category.name: DDoS & availability
category.description: Denial-of-service and availability incidents: volumetric and protocol floods, layer 7 abuse, reflection, extortion, and floods used as cover for intrusion.

playbooks.name: Volumetric UDP flood saturating internet uplinks
playbooks.summary: Use when edge links or firewall interfaces hit line rate with UDP traffic from many sources, causing packet loss and outages for internet-facing services.

preparation: Keep a signed scrubbing-service contract with a tested BGP or GRE diversion runbook
Record committed and burst bandwidth for each ISP circuit in the network inventory
Enable NetFlow or sFlow export from edge routers to a collector outside the attacked path
Pre-agree remote-triggered blackhole (RTBH) communities with each upstream provider
Store ISP NOC phone numbers and account IDs offline in the IR binder
identification: Confirm interface utilisation and drops on edge routers against the circuit baseline
Break flow data down by destination IP, UDP destination port, and packet size
Check whether source ports point to a reflection protocol such as 123, 1900, 11211, or 389
Identify which public prefixes and services are targeted versus collateral damage
Estimate peak Gbps and packets per second for the ISP and scrubbing provider
containment: Open a ticket with the upstream ISP and request UDP rate limits or ACLs at their edge
Swing the targeted prefix to the scrubbing provider by BGP announcement
Request RTBH of a single non-critical targeted /32 if it is sacrificing the whole circuit
Apply edge ACLs dropping unsolicited UDP to hosts that never serve UDP
eradication: Verify with the scrubbing provider that attack traffic is being dropped upstream
Remove any temporary broad ACLs that are also blocking legitimate UDP services
Confirm no internal host was used as part of the flood by checking outbound flows
recovery: Withdraw the scrubbing diversion only after traffic stays at baseline for an agreed window
Lift RTBH announcements and confirm reachability of the blackholed address
Monitor uplink utilisation and service health checks for 24 hours after withdrawal
lessons: Measure time from first saturation alert to scrubbing diversion
Decide whether always-on scrubbing is justified given attack frequency and size
Add an alert for UDP packets-per-second per destination above the baseline percentile
Review whether circuit capacity or provider diversity was the limiting factor

splunk.title: Top UDP destinations by bytes in 5-minute buckets
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes) as bytes count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.transport=udp by _time span=5m All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | sort - bytes | head 50

splunk.title: Reflection source ports hitting our prefixes
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(All_Traffic.bytes) as bytes dc(All_Traffic.src) as sources from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.transport=udp All_Traffic.src_port IN (19,53,123,161,389,1900,11211) by All_Traffic.src_port All_Traffic.dest | sort - bytes

splunk.title: UDP volume to target after scrubbing diversion
splunk.spl: index=netflow dest_ip=<target_ip> protocol=17 | timechart span=1m sum(bytes) as bytes dc(src_ip) as sources

playbooks.name: SYN flood exhausting firewall or load balancer state tables
playbooks.summary: Use when firewalls, load balancers, or servers report half-open connection exhaustion and new TCP sessions fail while bandwidth is not saturated.

preparation: Enable SYN cookies or SYN proxy on load balancers and firewalls in front of public VIPs
Baseline session table usage and new connections per second per VIP
Document session table limits and per-source connection thresholds for each edge device
Forward firewall session-table and threat logs to the SIEM with device health metrics
identification: Check firewall session table utilisation and half-open session counts per zone
Compare SYN to SYN-ACK and ACK ratios for the targeted VIP from flow or packet data
Capture a short pcap on the edge to see TTLs, window sizes, and spoofed source patterns
Determine whether sources are spoofed random addresses or a real botnet completing handshakes
List services behind the targeted VIP and the user impact of failed connections
containment: Turn on SYN proxy or SYN cookie mode for the targeted VIP on the load balancer
Lower embryonic connection timeouts on the firewall for the affected policy
Apply per-source SYN rate limits where sources are non-spoofed and repeat
Ask the ISP or scrubbing provider to filter TCP SYN to the target prefix
eradication: Confirm the session table has drained and half-open counts are back to baseline
Remove temporary per-source blocks that catch shared NAT or carrier-grade NAT ranges
Patch or tune devices that crashed or failed open under state exhaustion
recovery: Restore normal TCP timeouts after the attack subsides and watch for re-occurrence
Verify health checks and synthetic transactions succeed through each affected VIP
Review load balancer pool members for connection backlog or stuck workers
lessons: Add alerting on half-open session ratio per VIP rather than bandwidth only
Record whether SYN protection was already enabled and why it did not trigger
Evaluate moving stateful inspection behind a stateless scrubbing layer for public VIPs

splunk.title: Firewall session counts to targeted VIP by source /24
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=pan:traffic dest_ip=<target_vip> | eval src_net=replace(src_ip,"\.\d+$",".0/24") | stats count dc(src_ip) as hosts by src_net session_end_reason | sort - count | head 50

splunk.title: Incomplete TCP sessions over time
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=pan:traffic dest_ip=<target_vip> transport=tcp (app=incomplete OR session_end_reason=aged-out) | timechart span=1m count by dest_port

splunk.title: New connections per second after SYN proxy enabled
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest=<target_vip> All_Traffic.transport=tcp by _time span=1m All_Traffic.action

playbooks.name: HTTP/2 rapid reset style layer 7 flood
playbooks.summary: Use when web front ends or reverse proxies show extreme HTTP/2 stream creation and cancellation rates, CPU exhaustion, and timeouts with modest bandwidth.

preparation: Track reverse proxy and web server versions against HTTP/2 rapid reset vendor advisories
Log HTTP/2 stream resets and per-connection stream counts at the proxy or CDN
Configure max concurrent streams and per-connection request limits on proxies
Confirm the CDN or WAF provider offers emergency L7 mitigation and how to invoke it
identification: Check proxy metrics for RST_STREAM frames per connection and streams opened per second
Compare request rate at the edge with requests that reach origin applications
Identify client IPs or ASNs holding few connections but very high stream counts
Confirm the proxy build is patched for CVE-2023-44487 or note that it is vulnerable
Check whether the CDN already absorbed part of the flood or it is hitting origin directly
containment: Enable the CDN or WAF emergency L7 DDoS mode for the affected hostnames
Lower max concurrent streams and close connections that exceed a reset threshold
Temporarily disable HTTP/2 on exposed listeners and fall back to HTTP/1.1 if unpatched
Block or challenge source ASNs dominating stream creation
eradication: Upgrade reverse proxies and load balancers to versions with rapid reset mitigations
Remove emergency ASN blocks once traffic from those networks normalises
Verify no backend pools were left drained or scaled to zero during the incident
recovery: Re-enable HTTP/2 on patched listeners and watch reset ratios for regression
Validate latency and error rates on key pages through synthetic monitoring
Scale origin capacity back to normal after autoscaling surges
lessons: Add a detection for RST_STREAM ratio per client connection above baseline
Track patch lag for protocol-level DoS advisories on edge components
Document which mitigations the CDN applied automatically versus on request

splunk.title: Edge requests per client and status in 1-minute buckets
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.dest=<target_host> by _time span=1m Web.src Web.status | sort - count | head 100

splunk.title: Client IPs with high request rate and cancelled requests
splunk.spl: index=web sourcetype=nginx:plus:access OR sourcetype=haproxy:http host=<proxy_host> | stats count as reqs sum(eval(status=499)) as cancelled by clientip | eval cancel_ratio=round(cancelled/reqs,2) | where reqs>1000 | sort - cancel_ratio

splunk.title: Origin 5xx rate after mitigation
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.dest=<target_host> Web.status>=500 by _time span=5m Web.status

playbooks.name: Application-layer flood against the login endpoint
playbooks.summary: Use when the sign-in page or authentication API receives a sustained flood of requests that degrades login for real users, whether or not credentials are being tested.

preparation: Put the login endpoint behind a WAF with bot management and per-IP rate limits
Ensure the identity provider and app log failed and successful logins with client IP
Prepare a CAPTCHA or proof-of-work challenge that can be enabled on login quickly
Know the identity backend capacity limits such as LDAP binds or password hash cost
identification: Graph POST requests to the login path against the normal hourly baseline
Check whether submitted usernames are real accounts, indicating credential stuffing too
Identify user agents, JA3 or JA4 fingerprints, and ASNs common to the flood
Check directory or IdP CPU and authentication latency for backend exhaustion
Look for any successful logins from flood sources that need account follow-up
containment: Enable the login CAPTCHA or managed challenge for unauthenticated sessions
Apply WAF rate limits on the login path per IP and per fingerprint
Block flood ASNs or fingerprints that have no legitimate user population
Shed load by serving a static maintenance response for login only if the IdP is failing
eradication: Force password resets for accounts with successful logins from flood sources
Lock out or step-up MFA for usernames targeted heavily during the flood
Remove broad geo blocks that locked out legitimate users
recovery: Relax the challenge to risk-based mode once request rates return to baseline
Confirm login success rate and latency for real users through RUM or synthetic checks
Check account lockout queues and clear lockouts caused by the attack
lessons: Add an alert on login request rate and failure ratio per fingerprint
Review whether account lockout policy amplified the denial of service
Assess moving password verification behind a cheaper pre-auth throttle

splunk.title: Login path POSTs per source over time
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/login*" by _time span=5m Web.src | sort - count

splunk.title: Failed authentications by source with distinct users
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Authentication.user) as users from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.app=<login_app> by Authentication.src | where count>100 | sort - count

splunk.title: Successful logins from flood sources
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.src IN (<flood_ips>) by Authentication.user Authentication.src

playbooks.name: DNS amplification attack targeting our network
playbooks.summary: Use when large inbound DNS responses from many open resolvers flood your prefixes even though you sent no matching queries.

preparation: Confirm which hosts legitimately receive inbound UDP 53 responses, typically only resolvers
Enable flow export with packet size so large DNS responses are visible
Agree with the ISP how to apply an ACL for UDP source port 53 to a target prefix
identification: Confirm the flood is UDP source port 53 with large or fragmented packets
Check whether any internal resolver sent queries matching the response volume
Sample packets to identify the queried name and record type such as ANY or TXT
Count distinct reflector IPs and their ASNs for the ISP report
Identify which destination addresses are targeted and why, such as a public game or VPN IP
containment: Ask the upstream to drop UDP source port 53 to targets that are not DNS resolvers
Drop IP fragments to the target prefix at the edge if they are attack traffic
Divert the prefix to the scrubbing provider if the circuit remains saturated
eradication: Verify the upstream ACL is effective by checking edge counters and flow volume
Ensure internal resolvers still reach forwarders after source-port filtering
Close any exposed service on the target IP that made it attractive, such as an unused game port
recovery: Remove the upstream ACL after the agreed quiet period and watch for resumption
Test name resolution from internal resolvers and public services end to end
Report the reflector list to the ISP abuse team or a national CERT
lessons: Add a detection for inbound UDP 53 bytes to non-resolver destinations
Consider moving exposed services behind a provider that absorbs amplification
Record amplification factor and reflector count for trend reporting

splunk.title: Inbound DNS responses to non-resolver hosts
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes) as bytes dc(All_Traffic.src) as reflectors from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.transport=udp All_Traffic.src_port=53 NOT All_Traffic.dest IN (<resolver_ips>) by All_Traffic.dest | sort - bytes

splunk.title: Queried names and types in unsolicited responses
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=stream:dns dest_ip=<target_ip> message_type=RESPONSE | stats count sum(bytes_in) as bytes by query record_type | sort - count | head 20

splunk.title: Reflector ASN summary for ISP report
splunk.spl: index=netflow dest_ip=<target_ip> src_port=53 protocol=17 | stats sum(bytes) as bytes by src_ip | iplocation src_ip | stats sum(bytes) as bytes dc(src_ip) as reflectors by Country | sort - bytes

playbooks.name: Our DNS servers abused as reflectors in an amplification attack
playbooks.summary: Use when your authoritative or recursive DNS servers send large response volumes to a victim after receiving spoofed queries, or an abuse report says so.

preparation: Restrict recursion on resolvers to internal client ranges with ACLs
Enable response rate limiting (RRL) on authoritative DNS servers
Monitor outbound DNS response bytes per destination from each name server
Route ISP and CERT abuse mailbox reports to the SOC queue
identification: Read the abuse report and extract the victim IP, timestamps, and our server IPs cited
Check name server query logs for the repeated query name and type, such as ANY or DNSKEY
Confirm whether the server answers recursive queries from the internet
Measure outbound response volume per victim IP from flow data
Determine whether the source addresses are spoofed by checking for TCP follow-up or replies
containment: Disable open recursion on any resolver answering external clients
Enable or tighten RRL limits on authoritative servers for the abused query
Block or minimise ANY responses using the server's minimal-any style option
Apply an egress rate limit for UDP 53 responses toward the victim prefix
eradication: Fix the configuration management template that left recursion enabled
Audit every DNS server, including forgotten appliances, for open recursion
Remove large unneeded TXT records that maximise amplification
recovery: Re-test from an external vantage point that recursion is refused
Confirm legitimate authoritative answers are still served under RRL
Reply to the abuse reporter with the fix and timeline
lessons: Add a scheduled external scan for open resolvers on our address space
Alert on outbound DNS bytes to a single destination above baseline
Record time from abuse report receipt to remediation

splunk.title: Outbound DNS response volume per destination from our servers
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes) as bytes count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src IN (<dns_server_ips>) All_Traffic.src_port=53 by All_Traffic.dest | sort - bytes | head 20

splunk.title: Repeated query names from victim address
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=stream:dns src_ip=<victim_ip> | stats count avg(bytes_out) as avg_resp by query record_type dest_ip | sort - count

splunk.title: External recursive queries answered
splunk.spl: index=dns sourcetype=isc:bind:query NOT src IN (<internal_ranges>) | stats count by host query_type | sort - count

playbooks.name: Ransom DDoS extortion note received
playbooks.summary: Use when someone demands payment to avoid or stop a DDoS attack, often with a short demonstration flood, and you need to assess credibility and harden quickly.

preparation: Have a policy position on extortion payment agreed with legal and executives
Keep law enforcement and DDoS provider emergency contacts current
Maintain an inventory of public IPs, DNS names, and which are protected by scrubbing
identification: Preserve the extortion email with full headers and any payment wallet address
Check for a demonstration attack in the window the note claims and measure its size
Compare the note wording and wallet against threat intel on known RDDoS groups
Identify which services are named or implied and whether they are behind DDoS protection
Brief legal and executives on the demand, deadline, and credibility assessment
containment: Enable always-on scrubbing or CDN protection for named services before the deadline
Move unprotected origin IPs behind the provider or renumber them
Staff a bridge with network, the ISP, and the DDoS provider for the deadline window
Instruct staff not to reply to or engage with the extortion address
eradication: Report the demand and wallet to law enforcement with preserved evidence
Close exposed management interfaces on targeted IPs that increase attack surface
Share indicators with the sector ISAC
recovery: Keep heightened protection for at least two weeks past the deadline
Review service performance under always-on scrubbing for latency regressions
Communicate status to customer support in case of service degradation
lessons: Record whether the threat was carried out and at what scale
Review how many public assets lacked DDoS protection when the note arrived
Update the extortion response runbook with decision timings

splunk.title: Find the extortion email and other recipients
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user=<extortion_sender> OR All_Email.subject="*DDoS*" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.src_user

splunk.title: Traffic spike during claimed demonstration window
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes) as bytes from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest IN (<public_prefixes>) by _time span=1m All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.transport | where bytes>0 | sort - bytes

splunk.title: Traffic to targets around the deadline
splunk.spl: index=netflow dest_ip IN (<target_ips>) earliest=<deadline_minus_2h> latest=<deadline_plus_6h> | timechart span=1m sum(bytes) as bytes by dest_ip

playbooks.name: API exhaustion by bots scraping or hammering endpoints
playbooks.summary: Use when automated clients drive public or partner API endpoints into rate limits, quota exhaustion, or high cost, degrading service for legitimate integrations.

preparation: Enforce per-API-key and per-IP rate limits at the API gateway
Log API key, client ID, endpoint, and response time for every gateway request
Keep a contact list for partner integrations keyed by API client ID
identification: Rank API keys and client IPs by request count and backend latency contribution
Check whether the heavy client uses a valid key, a stolen partner key, or no key
Identify the endpoints hit and whether they are expensive, such as listing or export calls
Look for pagination walking or sequential ID enumeration indicating scraping
Quantify impact on error rates and cloud spend for affected backend services
containment: Throttle or suspend the abusive API key at the gateway
Add a tighter rate limit on the targeted expensive endpoint for all callers
Block or challenge the bot IP ranges at the WAF where no key is used
Contact the owning partner if a legitimate key is misbehaving
eradication: Rotate any partner key confirmed as leaked and issue a replacement
Require authentication on endpoints that were unintentionally anonymous
Cap page size and result count on listing endpoints
recovery: Restore normal quotas for legitimate clients and confirm their traffic resumes
Scale down any backend capacity added during the event
Verify backend queues and caches have drained
lessons: Add per-key anomaly alerting on request rate and distinct resource IDs
Review whether rate limits were set per endpoint cost or flat
Track cost incurred from the abuse for budget and contract discussions

splunk.title: Top API clients by request volume and latency
splunk.spl: index=api sourcetype=<api_gateway_sourcetype> | stats count avg(response_time) as avg_ms sum(response_time) as total_ms by api_key client_ip | sort - total_ms | head 25

splunk.title: Sequential ID enumeration on resource endpoints
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.url) as distinct_urls from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/*" by Web.src Web.http_user_agent | where distinct_urls>500 | sort - distinct_urls

splunk.title: 429 and 5xx rates by endpoint after throttling
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/*" (Web.status=429 OR Web.status>=500) by _time span=5m Web.status

playbooks.name: DDoS used as a smokescreen for an intrusion
playbooks.summary: Use when a DDoS coincides with suspicious authentication, data movement, or fraud, and you must keep investigating the quiet side while the flood draws attention.

preparation: Define in the DDoS runbook that a separate analyst monitors identity and data alerts
Ensure SIEM ingestion has capacity headroom so a flood does not drop security logs
Keep fraud and payments teams on the DDoS notification list
identification: Assign one analyst to the flood and one to hunt for concurrent intrusion activity
Check SIEM ingestion lag and dropped events during the flood window
Review privileged logins, MFA changes, and new admin accounts during the attack window
Look for unusual outbound data volume masked by the overall traffic spike
Ask fraud and payments teams for unusual transactions or wire changes in the window
containment: Disable accounts and revoke sessions showing suspicious activity during the flood
Block outbound destinations receiving unexplained data transfers
Freeze high-risk payment changes until reviewed
Keep DDoS mitigation running without letting staff disable security controls to recover speed
eradication: Run full compromise assessment on hosts tied to the suspicious activity
Reset credentials and API keys used by the intrusion
Re-enable any IDS or WAF rule sets that were put in bypass for performance
recovery: Backfill SIEM data that was delayed or dropped and re-run correlation searches
Verify no security tools were left in fail-open or bypass after the flood
Confirm with fraud and payments that frozen transactions were reviewed and released or reversed
lessons: Record which security controls were bypassed for availability and who approved it
Add a correlation rule pairing DDoS alerts with privileged or financial events
Size SIEM and log pipelines for attack-volume traffic

splunk.title: Privileged and admin changes during the flood window
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where earliest=<flood_start> latest=<flood_end> (All_Changes.object_category=user OR All_Changes.object_category=group) by All_Changes.user All_Changes.action All_Changes.object

splunk.title: Large outbound transfers during the flood
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as out from datamodel=Network_Traffic where earliest=<flood_start> latest=<flood_end> All_Traffic.direction=outbound by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest | where out>100000000 | sort - out

splunk.title: Ingestion lag by sourcetype during the attack
splunk.spl: index=* earliest=<flood_start> latest=<flood_end> | eval lag=_indextime-_time | stats avg(lag) as avg_lag max(lag) as max_lag count by sourcetype | sort - max_lag

playbooks.name: Attack bypassing CDN or WAF by hitting exposed origin
playbooks.summary: Use when floods or exploits arrive directly at origin servers instead of through the CDN or WAF because the origin IP is discoverable and accepts direct traffic.

preparation: Restrict origin ingress to the CDN provider's published IP ranges
Keep origin IPs out of public DNS records, mail headers, and certificate SAN history
Use authenticated origin pulls or a shared secret header from the CDN
identification: Compare origin access logs for client IPs that are not CDN ranges
Check whether direct hits carry the CDN secret header or mTLS client cert
Search passive DNS and certificate transparency for leaked origin IP history
Look for MX, SPF, or subdomain records that resolve to the origin network
Confirm whether the flood volume reaching origin exceeds what the CDN reports
containment: Apply origin firewall rules allowing only CDN ranges on 80 and 443
Enable authenticated origin pulls and reject requests without the CDN credential
Ask the hosting provider to null-route the origin IP if it is overwhelmed
eradication: Move the origin to a new IP that has never appeared in public DNS
Remove DNS records and mail paths that disclose the origin network
Rotate the origin shared secret header
recovery: Point the CDN at the new origin and validate cache and health checks
Verify direct requests to the new origin time out from an external host
Decommission the old exposed origin IP after traffic has fully moved
lessons: Add a detection for non-CDN source IPs in origin access logs
Scan certificate transparency for new certificates naming origin hostnames
Review why origin lockdown was missing from the deployment checklist

splunk.title: Origin requests from non-CDN source ranges
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.dest=<origin_host> by Web.src | lookup cdn_ip_ranges cidr AS Web.src OUTPUT provider | where isnull(provider) | sort - count

splunk.title: Origin traffic volume direct vs via CDN
splunk.spl: index=web host=<origin_host> | eval via_cdn=if(isnotnull(cdn_secret_header),"cdn","direct") | timechart span=5m count by via_cdn

splunk.title: Direct connections to new origin after lockdown
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest=<new_origin_ip> All_Traffic.action=allowed by All_Traffic.src | lookup cdn_ip_ranges cidr AS All_Traffic.src OUTPUT provider | where isnull(provider)

playbooks.name: Carrier-level outage or attack: determining which
playbooks.summary: Use when connectivity or reachability fails broadly and you must quickly tell an ISP, BGP, or cloud provider outage apart from a DDoS before choosing a response.

preparation: Subscribe to ISP and cloud provider status pages and maintenance notifications
Set up external synthetic monitoring from several networks and regions
Configure BGP monitoring for our prefixes to alert on withdrawals and hijacks
Keep out-of-band access to edge routers that does not depend on the primary circuit
identification: Check edge router BGP session state and received route counts with each upstream
Compare interface traffic: near zero suggests outage, line rate suggests attack
Check public BGP looking glasses and route collectors for our prefix visibility
Review provider status pages and outage community lists for the affected region
Test reachability from external probes on multiple carriers to isolate the failing path
containment: Shift traffic to the secondary ISP by de-preferencing the failing upstream
Escalate to the carrier NOC with traceroutes and BGP evidence
Invoke the DDoS runbook only if flow data shows attack traffic at saturation
eradication: Confirm the carrier root cause statement and ticket closure
Correct any route filter, RPKI, or configuration error on our side that contributed
Report a BGP hijack to the offending ASN and upstreams if prefixes were announced elsewhere
recovery: Restore normal BGP preferences once the primary path is stable
Verify all public services from external probes on each carrier
Check that VPN tunnels and SaaS connectors re-established after failover
lessons: Measure time spent deciding outage versus attack and what data settled it
Review whether failover to the secondary ISP was automatic or manual
Publish ROAs for our prefixes if RPKI was missing

playbooks.name: Telephony denial of service flooding call centre lines
playbooks.summary: Use when automated or spoofed calls flood inbound phone numbers, SIP trunks, or contact-centre queues so real callers cannot get through.

preparation: Log call detail records from the SBC and contact-centre platform to the SIEM
Agree with the telephony carrier how to request upstream call filtering
Configure SBC call admission control and per-source SIP rate limits
Prepare an alternative public number or callback channel for emergencies
identification: Pull call detail records showing call volume, duration, and calling numbers per trunk
Identify patterns such as short silent calls, repeated ANI, or sequential spoofed numbers
Check SBC logs for SIP INVITE floods from internet sources outside the carrier
Confirm which DIDs and queues are targeted and the abandoned-call rate for real customers
Check whether the flood follows an extortion demand or a public dispute
containment: Ask the carrier to block or rate limit the offending calling patterns upstream
Enable an IVR challenge such as press-a-digit to filter robocalls
Restrict SIP signalling on the SBC to carrier IP ranges only
Route priority callers to an alternate number published to key customers
eradication: Close direct internet SIP exposure on PBX or SBC interfaces
Report the flood to the carrier and law enforcement with CDR evidence
Remove compromised or abused SIP credentials and rotate trunk passwords
recovery: Remove the IVR challenge when call patterns return to normal
Review contact-centre staffing and queue backlog created by the flood
Confirm emergency and outbound calling were unaffected
lessons: Add an alert on calls per minute and short-call ratio per DID
Document carrier response time and filtering capabilities
Evaluate a voice-firewall or carrier TDoS protection service

splunk.title: Calls per minute by DID with short-call ratio
splunk.spl: index=voip sourcetype=<cdr_sourcetype> | eval short=if(duration<10,1,0) | timechart span=1m count sum(short) as short_calls by called_number

splunk.title: Top calling numbers and their call counts
splunk.spl: index=voip sourcetype=<cdr_sourcetype> called_number=<target_did> | stats count avg(duration) as avg_dur by calling_number | sort - count | head 50

splunk.title: SIP INVITEs from non-carrier sources
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (5060,5061) All_Traffic.dest=<sbc_ip> by All_Traffic.src | lookup carrier_sip_ranges cidr AS All_Traffic.src OUTPUT carrier | where isnull(carrier) | sort - count

playbooks.name: Email bombing of a user's mailbox
playbooks.summary: Use when a user suddenly receives thousands of subscription confirmations or junk emails, which often hides a fraud alert and precedes fake help-desk calls.

preparation: Configure mail gateway thresholds for inbound messages per recipient per hour
Warn staff that IT never cold-calls or messages about spam floods to request remote access
Ensure message trace and mailbox audit logs are retained and searchable
identification: Run message trace for the user to count inbound messages and sending domains per hour
Search the flood for legitimate security notices such as bank, payroll, or password resets
Ask the user about any calls or chat messages claiming to be IT support
Check whether the user installed remote support tools such as Quick Assist after the flood
Check the user's account for new inbox rules, MFA changes, or unfamiliar sign-ins
containment: Apply a temporary transport rule quarantining bulk confirmation mail to the user
Block external Teams or chat contact from unknown tenants to the targeted user
Isolate the endpoint if a remote support tool session was granted to the caller
Revoke sessions and reset the password if any credential was shared
eradication: Remove inbox rules or forwarding added during the flood
Uninstall unauthorised remote access tools and review persistence on the endpoint
Report sign-up abuse to the newsletter services used for the flood
recovery: Release legitimate messages from quarantine after review with the user
Remove the temporary transport rule once inbound volume is normal
Check with finance or HR for any account changes the flood may have hidden
lessons: Add alerting on per-recipient inbound message spikes
Correlate email bomb alerts with external chat and remote-tool launches
Update awareness training with the email-bomb then fake-helpdesk pattern

splunk.title: Inbound messages per hour to the targeted user
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count dc(All_Email.src_user) as senders from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient=<target_user> by _time span=1h | sort _time

splunk.title: Security notices hidden in the flood
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient=<target_user> (All_Email.subject="*password*" OR All_Email.subject="*verify*" OR All_Email.subject="*payment*" OR All_Email.subject="*transfer*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject

splunk.title: Remote support tools launched on the user's endpoint
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest=<user_host> Processes.process_name IN (quickassist.exe,AnyDesk.exe,TeamViewer.exe,ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe) by Processes.process_name Processes.user _time

playbooks.name: Resource exhaustion via expensive search or report queries
playbooks.summary: Use when a small number of requests to search, filter, or reporting features drive databases or search clusters to full CPU, causing slowdowns site-wide.

preparation: Enable slow query logging on databases and search clusters with client attribution
Set query timeouts and maximum result windows in the application and search engine
Tag application logs with request ID so slow queries map to web requests
identification: Pull the slow query log and rank query shapes by total execution time
Map slow queries back to request URLs, user accounts, and client IPs
Check for wildcard, regex, deep pagination, or unbounded date range parameters
Determine whether requests come from authenticated users, a scraper, or a single tenant
Check database connection pool saturation and lock waits
containment: Kill long-running queries matching the abusive pattern
Rate limit or disable the expensive search parameter at the WAF or feature flag
Suspend the account or API key driving the queries
Route reporting traffic to a read replica if available
eradication: Add server-side limits on page depth, wildcard prefix, and date range
Add or fix indexes for the query shape that was abused
Require authentication for the expensive search feature
recovery: Re-enable the feature with limits and watch query latency
Confirm replication lag and cache hit rates have recovered
Restore suspended accounts after confirming their usage was legitimate or contracted
lessons: Add an alert on slow query rate per client or account
Load test search endpoints with worst-case parameters before release
Record whether WAF signatures could have caught the parameter pattern

splunk.title: Slow requests by URL and client
splunk.spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined uri_path="*/search*" | stats count avg(response_time) as avg_rt max(response_time) as max_rt by clientip uri_path | where avg_rt>2000 | sort - avg_rt

splunk.title: Database slow queries by shape
splunk.spl: index=db sourcetype=mysql:slowquery OR sourcetype=postgresql | rex field=_raw "(?i)(?<qshape>select .{0,120})" | stats count sum(query_time) as total_time by qshape user | sort - total_time | head 20

splunk.title: Search parameter patterns in web logs
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/search*" (Web.url="*page=*" OR Web.url="*q=*%2A*") by Web.src Web.url | sort - count | head 50

playbooks.name: Flood against game servers or live streaming service
playbooks.summary: Use when game servers, matchmaking, or live stream ingest are hit by floods, often targeting specific players, tournaments, or streamers, causing disconnects.

preparation: Host game and ingest servers with providers offering UDP-aware DDoS filtering
Hide game server IPs from clients where possible using relays or proxies
Collect per-server player count, tick rate, and packet loss metrics
Prepare a plan to migrate matches or events to backup regions
identification: Identify targeted server IPs and whether they host a particular match or player
Check whether flood packets mimic game protocol traffic or are generic UDP
Correlate disconnect spikes with specific player accounts or lobbies
Check if a streamer or tournament schedule leaked server addresses
Measure packet loss, tick rate, and player disconnect rate on affected servers
containment: Enable provider game-protocol filtering profiles for targeted servers
Move active matches to fresh server IPs not yet known to the attacker
Rate limit unauthenticated connection requests to matchmaking services
Pause or reschedule high-profile events if mitigation is insufficient
eradication: Suspend player accounts linked to leaking server IPs or running booter services
Remove server IP disclosure from client UI, logs, or APIs
Report booter services and evidence to the provider and law enforcement
recovery: Return matches to standard regions once traffic returns to baseline
Compensate or communicate with affected players and streamers
Verify stream ingest bitrates and dropped frames are normal
lessons: Add per-server UDP pps alerts tied to player disconnect metrics
Review how attackers learned target IPs and close that path
Track repeat targeting by player or event to anticipate future floods

splunk.title: UDP pps to game server fleet by server
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.packets) as pkts sum(All_Traffic.bytes) as bytes from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.transport=udp All_Traffic.dest IN (<game_server_ips>) by _time span=1m All_Traffic.dest | sort - pkts

splunk.title: Player disconnects by server and lobby
splunk.spl: index=game sourcetype=<game_server_sourcetype> event=player_disconnect | timechart span=1m count by server_id

splunk.title: Players present on every attacked server
splunk.spl: index=game sourcetype=<game_server_sourcetype> event=player_join server_ip IN (<attacked_ips>) | stats dc(server_ip) as servers values(server_ip) as ips by player_id | where servers>=2 | sort - servers
